::: {.notes}
Problem 1: one experiment, and the clock.
:::

## When do we stop? {background-color="#f3e3c1" .content .sec1}

::: {.cbody}
::: {.incremental}
- The checkout redesign: when do we stop, and decide whether to ship it?
- Stop early: a decent decision, quickly.
- Wait: a better decision, slowly.
- Wrong comes in sizes: shipping a 0.1% loss is not shipping a 5% loss.
:::

[Every platform answers with a named test and a few parameters.  The question is what those parameters trade.]{.fragment .below-note}
:::

::: {.notes}
Back to the checkout redesign.  Revenue per visitor accrues every day, and every day someone asks whether we can decide yet.  Stop early and we get a decent decision quickly; wait and we get a better one slowly.  Wrong also comes in sizes: shipping a redesign that loses a tenth of a per cent is not shipping one that loses five.  Every platform answers with a named test and a few parameters.  This section asks what those parameters trade.
:::

## Two axes, kept apart {background-color="#f3e3c1" .content .sec1}

::: {.cbody}
::: {.incremental}
- A procedure $P=(\tau,\varphi)$: $\tau$ a stopping time, then $\varphi(\mathcal X)\in\{A,B\}$.
- Average over $G$, the distribution of true effects across experiments:
  $$S(P)=\mathbb{E}_{\theta\sim G}\,\mathbb{E}_\theta[\tau],\qquad R(P)=\mathbb{E}_{\theta\sim G}\big[\,|\theta|\;\mathbb{P}_\theta\{\varphi(\mathcal X)\neq\varphi^*(\theta)\}\big].$$
- The frontier, over all procedures: $\Phi(s)=\inf\{R(P):S(P)\le s\}$.
- Name a point: cap $R$ and minimise $S$, or cap $S$ and minimise $R$.
:::

[No exchange rate between days and revenue is assumed.]{.fragment .below-note}
:::

::: {.notes}
$\varphi$ is the rule from the textbook slide, $\varphi^*$ is the oracle, and $\tau$ is the stopping time from the sequential-test slide.  What is new is the score.  Two numbers, both averaged over $G$, the distribution of true effects across the platform's experiments: speed, the expected sample size, so smaller is faster; and regret, which is zero when the sign is right and $|\theta|$ when it is wrong.  The frontier $\Phi$ is the best regret achievable at each speed, over all procedures.  A point on it is chosen by capping one axis.  No rate of exchange between days and revenue is assumed.
:::

:::

[Computed, not schematic: one knob traces a curve; two knobs fill a region, whose lower edge is the best tuning.  Fixed horizon has sample size and level: the grey edge is the sign rule, and the band reaches the 5% level.  SPRT is one knob; mixture SPRT and expected loss show lower edges.  $\Phi$ is the best of all procedures.  Linear scales; model and units in the appendix.]{.p1-caption}

[For $S\le50$ the SPRT is within 16% of $\Phi$; the others lose up to a factor of 2 to 8, and every gap is widening.]{.fragment .below-note fragment-index=4}
:::

::: {.notes}
One knob traces a curve.  Two knobs fill a region: its lower edge is the best tuning, while points above are attainable and worse.  Fixed horizon has two knobs, sample size and level.  Grey is the sign-rule edge, and the shaded band runs to the 5% level.  [click] The SPRT has one boundary and is a curve; mixture SPRT and expected loss show only their lower edges.  [click] Their menu offers the lower envelope: here, the SPRT throughout.  [click] Dashed $\Phi$ is the best any procedure can do, computed by backward induction.  [click] Up to $S=50$ the SPRT is within 16% of it; on this loss the others lose up to a factor of two to eight, and every gap is widening.  [Optional: Where do platforms sit?  One 20-million-user Bing test is $S\approx0.02$, off the left edge, where all four lower edges are within 7% of $\Phi$.  Revenue with a 1% spread of effects reaches $S=50$ at about 40 million visitors, where the SPRT needs 8% more traffic than the optimum and the fixed sign rule eight times as much.]
:::

## The frontier is a Bayes problem {background-color="#f3e3c1" .content .sec1}

::: {.cbody}
::: {.incremental}
- Mix two procedures by an independent coin at time $0$: the attainable set $\mathcal{A}=\{(S(P),R(P)):P\}$ is convex.
- So each point of $\Phi$ supports a line of slope $-c$: it minimises, for some $c>0$,
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$
R(P)+c\,S(P)=\mathbb{E}_{\theta\sim G}\Big[\,|\theta|\,\mathbb{P}_\theta\{\varphi(\mathcal X)\neq\varphi^*(\theta)\}+c\,\mathbb{E}_\theta[\tau]\,\Big].
$$
:::

::: {.incremental}
- This is the Bayes sequential problem: prior $G$, loss $|\theta|$, cost $c$ per observation (1949).
:::

[No price was assumed; the frontier prices speed anyway, at $c$ per observation.]{.fragment .below-note}

[Kenneth Arrow, David Blackwell, and Meyer Girshick 1949.]{.cite}
:::

::: {.notes}
The dashed curve is computable because a coin flip at time zero averages two procedures' speeds and regrets: the attainable set $\mathcal A$ is convex, so every point of $\Phi$ supports a line of slope $-c$, i.e. minimises $R+cS$ for some price $c$ per observation.  Unpacked, that priced problem is exactly a Bayes sequential decision problem: a prior $G$ on $\theta$, a loss $|\theta|$ for the wrong sign, and a cost $c$ per observation, due to Kenneth Arrow, David Blackwell, and Meyer Girshick, 1949.  [click] No price on days was assumed two slides ago; the frontier prices it anyway, at $c$ per observation, once you ask for the best speed at a given regret.
:::

## The minimiser is classical {background-color="#f3e3c1" .content .sec1}

::: {.cbody}
::: {.incremental}
- Two-point prior: the minimiser of $R+cS$ is Wald's SPRT (1948).
- Normal prior, loss $|\theta|$: the minimiser is Chernoff's procedure for the sign of a normal mean (1961).  That is the dashed curve.
:::

[These results are classical.  The frontier is the benchmark.]{.fragment .below-note}

[Abraham Wald and Jacob Wolfowitz 1948; Herman Chernoff 1961.]{.cite}
:::

::: {.notes}
Two theorems, not a derivation.  [click] For two simple hypotheses, Abraham Wald and Jacob Wolfowitz (1948): among all tests with those two error probabilities, the SPRT minimises the expected sample size under both.  That is the minimiser of $R+cS$ for a two-point prior.  [click] For a normal prior and loss $|\theta|$ on the wrong sign, the minimiser is Herman Chernoff's 1961 procedure for the sign of a normal mean.  The dashed curve is that procedure, one point for each cost $c$.  Under this prior the SPRT is a different rule; the previous slide already says it stays within 16% up to $S=50$.  [Optional: Herman Chernoff died this July, at 103.]  [click] These results are classical.  The frontier is the benchmark.
:::

## What platforms ship {background-color="#f3e3c1" .content .sec1}

::: {.cbody}
::: {.incremental}
- A small menu, per the public documentation:
  - Mixture SPRT: Optimizely's default, always valid; an opt-in at Statsig.
  - Sequential by default; fixed, Bayesian, or hybrid when power is scarce: Eppo.
  - Expected loss below a 'threshold of caring': Chris Stucchio's SmartStats at VWO, 2015.
- One industry attempt: simulate each family over its parameters, let the user cap one axis, and read the point off the envelope.
:::

[Vendors ship families and defaults.  Nobody, as far as we know, ships $\Phi$.]{.fragment .below-note}

[Vendor documentation, checked October 2026; Chris Stucchio 2015; Ramesh Johari et al. 2022.]{.cite}
:::

::: {.notes}
What industry ships is a small menu of descendants.  Herbert Robbins's mixture SPRT, made into always-valid $p$-values by Ramesh Johari, Leonid Pekelis, and David Walsh, is Optimizely's default and an opt-in at Statsig, valid there for reads before the target date, alongside an SPRT; Eppo defaults to sequential.  Chris Stucchio's SmartStats, VWO's engine from 2015, stopped when expected loss fell below a threshold of caring; VWO, now Wingify, has moved new campaigns to a probability-to-beat-baseline rule.  In marketing, Elea McDonnell Feit and Ron Berman's test and roll picks a fixed sample to maximise profit over a finite rollout.  One industry attempt simulated every family over its parameters and let the user cap one axis: the picture two slides back, without the dashed curve.
:::

## What false-positive control costs {background-color="#f3e3c1" .content .sec1 .fit}

::: {.cbody}
::: {.incremental}
- Fixed sample, $\varphi_k(\mathcal X)=A$ iff $\hat\theta\ge k\operatorname{se}$.  One-sided level $\mathbb{P}_0\{\varphi_k(\mathcal X)=A\}=5\%$ means $k=1.645$
:::

:::

::: {.incremental}
- $\theta<0$: the wrong sign is rare.  $\theta>0$: the worst regret is five times the sign rule's.
- Symmetric $G$: the sign rule $k=0$ minimises $R$.
:::

[Level control is insurance on one side, paid for in regret on the other.]{.fragment .below-note}

[Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson 1933.]{.cite}
:::

::: {.notes}
So far the talk has scored only speed and regret.  The textbook scores a test differently: by its level, the chance of choosing A when there is no effect.  Take one fixed sample and a threshold $k$ on $\hat\theta$ in standard errors.  [click] At a 5% level, $k=1.645$.  [click] On the left, the probability of choosing A as the true effect varies; the level-controlled test is shifted right.  On the right, the regret: the size of the effect times the chance of the wrong sign.  Left of zero, the 5% test is nearly perfect.  Right of zero, it keeps B for real improvements, and its worst regret is about five times the sign rule's: $0.84$ against $0.17$ standard errors.  [click] If the true effects are symmetric about zero, the posterior mean has the sign of $\hat\theta$, so the sign rule is Bayes for regret at this sample size.  [click] Level control buys protection on one side and pays for it on the other.
:::

## What does all this mean in the real world? {background-color="#f3e3c1" .content .sec1}

::: {.cbody}
::: {.incremental}
- $\theta$: the difference in revenue per visitor, in dollars.
- $S$: visitors spent testing.  At $v$ visitors a day, $S/v$ days.
- $R$: dollars per visitor lost to a wrong call.  After launch, $R\,v$ dollars a day.
- [Unanswered:]{.unanswered} Is $|\theta|$ the best choice of loss?  Why not $\theta^2$, or some other formulation?
:::

[What is the right choice for a business?]{.fragment .below-note}

[Dollars and days are real; the loss that turns them into one number is a choice.]{.fragment .below-note}

[Nicholas Larsen et al. 2024 (the checkout page in dollars); Ron Kohavi, Diane Tang, and Ya Xu 2020 (the overall evaluation criterion).]{.cite}
:::

::: {.notes}
Back to the checkout page, in dollars and days.  [click] The effect $\theta$ is the difference in revenue per visitor, so it is already in dollars per visitor.  [click] Speed $S$ is visitors spent before deciding; at $v$ visitors a day, that is $S/v$ days.  [click] Regret $R$ is the expected dollars per visitor lost to choosing the wrong page, and everyone who arrives after the decision pays it: $R$ times $v$ dollars a day, for as long as the decision stands.  Both axes are already real money.  [click] What is not settled is the loss itself.  $|\theta|$ is linear and symmetric, chosen because it makes the problem clean, not because the business asked for it.  $\theta^2$ is the obvious alternative, and there are others: a loss worse on one side than the other, a fixed cost to ship, a discount for effects that fade.  Each is a different Bayes problem, with a different frontier.  [click] What is the right choice for a business?  [click] Dollars and days are real; the loss that turns them into one number is a choice.
:::

## [Unanswered:]{.unanswered} How far is the menu from $\Phi$? {background-color="#f3e3c1" .content .sec1}

::: {.cbody}
::: {.incremental}
- The menu: the few tests a platform ships.  $\Phi$: the best of all procedures.
- At the same speed, the menu's regret sits above $\Phi$.  For normal $G$, the SPRT is within 16% up to $S=50$; the others are 2 to 8 times $\Phi$.
- Real-world effects are fat-tailed, not normal, and $G$ is not known.
- Is there a short menu that stays close to $\Phi$ for every plausible $G$, at the speeds platforms run?
:::

[Why industry cares: the gap above $\Phi$, times visitors a day, is dollars left on the table.]{.fragment .below-note}

[Herman Chernoff 1965 (best SPRT against Bayes, for one prior); Eduardo Azevedo et al. 2020 (fat tails).]{.cite}
:::

::: {.notes}
So the open question is not the frontier; it is the menu.  [click] A platform ships a few named tests; $\Phi$ is the best any procedure can do.  [click] At the same speed, the menu always loses something.  For a normal prior the SPRT is close, within 16% up to $S=50$, and the others are two to eight times worse; the gap widens with speed.  [click] But real effects are not normal: Eduardo Azevedo and co-authors found extremely fat tails, and in any case the platform does not know $G$.  [click] So the theorem we want is a worst case: over a class of priors, over the speeds a platform actually runs, for menus of one-knob tests, since tuning every knob to $G$ just gives back the Bayes rule.  Herman Chernoff's 1965 comparison of the best SPRT with the Bayes rule is in exactly this direction, for one prior.  As far as we know, nobody has the theorem.  [click] Why industry cares: the gap above $\Phi$ is regret per visitor, and the real-world slide turned regret into dollars a day.  That gap is money left on the table, every day the decision stands.
:::

## [Unanswered:]{.unanswered} The prior, the clock, the contract {background-color="#f3e3c1" .content .sec1}

::: {.cbody}
::: {.incremental}
- Prior.  We assumed $G$ known.  In practice it is fitted to past experiments, which may keep only the winners.  What is the best procedure when $G$ is only roughly known?
- Clock.  $S$ counts visitors; the business counts days.  Traffic varies, revenue arrives late, and novelty fades.  Which of these change the frontier, not just its units?
- Contract.  We scored one metric, revenue.  A page can win on it and lose on refunds, latency, or support contacts.  How does $\Phi$ change when a second metric must not fall?
:::

[Why industry cares: each one moves the platform's test off $\Phi$, and every gap is dollars left on the table.]{.fragment .below-note}

[Mårten Schultzberg and Mattias Frånberg 2026 (priors that fail to calibrate); James Berger 1985 ($\Gamma$-minimax).]{.cite}
:::

::: {.notes}
Three more assumptions the model made, each of which the business breaks.  [click] The prior.  Everything so far assumed $G$ known.  It is fitted to the platform's own history; if that history keeps only winners, or pools unlike programmes, Mårten Schultzberg and Mattias Frånberg show the fitted prior can fail to calibrate however large the corpus.  The natural fix is a worst case over a class of priors, the $\Gamma$-minimax frontier of James Berger's 1985 book.  [click] The clock.  Speed counts visitors; the business counts days.  Known traffic only relabels the axis.  Revenue that arrives late, and a novelty effect that fades, change the problem itself.  [click] The contract.  The model scores one metric.  A checkout page can raise revenue and raise refunds, latency, or support contacts, and a team will refuse to ship unless that second metric holds.  That is a constraint on the same frontier: how far above $\Phi$ does it push the test?  Ron Kohavi, Diane Tang, and Ya Xu call these guardrails, in the overall evaluation criterion already cited.  [click] Why industry cares: a misfitted prior, a wrong clock, or a guardrail that must not fall each pushes the platform's test off $\Phi$, and each gap is paid in dollars on every visitor after launch.
:::
